Consider the following singly linked list where the head points to the first node of the linked list.
$$2 \rightarrow 4 \rightarrow 6 \rightarrow 8 \rightarrow 10 \rightarrow \textsf{NULL}$$
If we execute the following code on the above-linked list then what will be the final linked list?

Node* recursive_swap(Node* head) {
    if (head == NULL || head->next == NULL)
        return head;

    Node* first = head;
    Node* second = head->next;

    first->next = recursive_swap(second->next);
    second->next = first;

    return second;
}
  1. $2 \rightarrow 4 \rightarrow 6 \rightarrow 8 \rightarrow 10 \rightarrow$ NULL
  2. $4 \rightarrow 2 \rightarrow 8 \rightarrow 6 \rightarrow 10 \rightarrow$ NULL
  3. $2 \rightarrow 6 \rightarrow 4 \rightarrow 8 \rightarrow 10 \rightarrow$ NULL

In a game where two players take turns picking cards from either end of a sequence $s_{1}, s_{2}, \ldots, s_{n}$, each card $s_{i}$ has a value $v_{i}$. Both players aim to maximize their total value and play optimally.

Define $V(i, j)$ as the maximum score the first player can achieve on a sub-sequence from index $i$ to $j$, aiming to maximize their score while minimizing the opponent's.

  3. $V(i, j)=\max \left(V(i+1, j)-v_{i}, V(i, j-1)-v_{j}\right)$
  4. $V(i, j)=\min (V(i+1, j), V(i, j-1))$

Two transactions are "not-interleaved" in a schedule if every action of one transaction precedes every action of the other.
We say that a transaction $T$ precedes a transaction $U$ in a schedule $S$ if they are not interleaved, and all actions of $T$ precedes all actions of $U$ in $S.$

Note that if $T$ and $U$ are the Only transactions in $S$, then saying $T$ precedes $U$ is the same as saying that $S$ is the serial schedule $(T, U).$

However, if $S$ involves transactions other than $T$ and $U,$ then $S$ might not be a serial schedule, in fact, because of the effect of other transactions, $S$ might not even be conflict-serializable.

Consider a conflict-serializable schedule $S$ in which transactions $\mathrm{T1}$ and $T2$ are not interleaved in $S,$ and $T1$ precedes $T2$ in $S.$ The Schedule $S$ may include more than $2$ transactions.

Which of the following must be true for $S?$

  1. In any serial schedule conflict equivalent to $\mathrm{S}, \mathrm{T} 1$ precedes $T2.$
  2. In any serial schedule conflict equivalent to $\mathrm{S}, \mathrm{T} 2$ precedes $T1.$
  3. There exists at least one serial schedule conflict equivalent to $S$ in which $T1$ precedes $T2.$
  4. None of the above is necessarily true.
